Neonatal Spix’s macaws (Cyanopsitta spixii) emerge from the egg with a modest body mass, a consequence of the finite resources packaged within the calcareous shell during incubation. Hatchlings typically weigh approximately 15.2 grams [Wwb = approximately 15.2 grams], a value that marks the starting point for a period of rapid mass gain fueled entirely by parental provisioning. This developmental trajectory is defined by a series of well-characterized milestones, the timing of which is tightly coupled to the thermal environment. At the incubation temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], the embryo completes its development and the age at hatching spans between 24 and 28 days (24-28 days) [ab = 24-28 days], with a central estimate of 26 days [ab = 26 days]. The narrowness of this range suggests strong canalization of the developmental program under stable incubation conditions, consistent with patterns observed in other medium-sized parrots. Following hatching, the altricial nestling enters a phase of intense somatic growth, wherein daily mass increments are prioritized to build the structural framework necessary for eventual independence. The wet weight at birth establishes the baseline from which subsequent growth trajectories are measured.

The nestling period of Cyanopsitta spixii culminates in a critical transition: fledging, or the achievement of the first sustained flight. Under the typical metabolic body temperature of active adults (41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]), young macaws depart the nest cavity approximately 70 days after hatching [tx = approximately 70 days after hatching]. This age represents the culmination of a developmental program involving feather maturation, pectoral muscle development, and the neurological coordination required for controlled aerial locomotion. Observations of captive-reared individuals indicate that the fledgling period is prolonged relative to many smaller parrot species, a pattern that corresponds to the larger adult body size of the Spix’s macaw. During the final weeks before nest departure, the chick undergoes a pronounced increase in mass and begins to exercise its wings within the cavity’s entrance, a behavior termed branching. The supportive thermal regime provided by the parents remains essential throughout this phase, as the chick’s own endothermic capacity is still developing.

Sexual maturation in Spix’s macaw occurs considerably later than fledging, reflecting the extended period of social learning and nutritional independence required before the onset of reproductive competence. Gonadal development is completed by approximately 210 days after hatching [tp = approximately 210 days after hatching] at the typical active body temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. This age, however, does not correspond to the onset of breeding; instead, it marks the point at which the bird is physiologically capable of reproduction. The delay between puberty and first reproduction is a well-documented feature among large psittacines, where the acquisition of a territory, the formation of a stable pair bond, and the mastery of complex foraging skills precede any attempt at nesting. In the wild, this interval can be considerably longer than the minimum physiological threshold. The total body mass at this stage approaches the asymptotic adult value, ensuring that the energetic demands of gamete production can be met without compromising somatic condition.

The first successful breeding event of a Spix’s macaw is not opportunistic but represents a significant life-history threshold that integrates physiological readiness with ecological opportunity. Under the typical active metabolic temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C], the time since birth at first brood is approximately 730 days [tR = approximately 730 days]. This delay relative to puberty reflects the dual constraints of territory establishment and the necessity of accumulating sufficient experience to successfully incubate eggs and provision young. Once a pair begins reproducing, females typically lay between 2 and 3 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 2 and 3 eggs per clutch], a modest clutch size that is characteristic of large-bodied psittacines exhibiting K-selected life-history strategies. The frequency with which clutches are produced annually has been estimated at approximately 0.67 clutches per year [F_R_i = approximately 0.67 clutches per year], although this value may be sensitive to rainfall patterns and food availability in the arid Caatinga habitat. The maximum reproductive rate, therefore, integrates both the per-clutch output and the annual laying frequency.

Maximum lifespan in Spix’s macaw, as inferred from captive records and extrapolated to wild conditions, is considerable for a bird of its body size. At a body temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C], the maximum longevity is estimated at 27 years [am = 27 years], a value that underscores the species’ position on the slow end of the life-history continuum. This extended lifespan is accompanied by a high asymptotic body mass; adults attain an ultimate wet weight of approximately 280 grams [Wwi = approximately 280 grams], which represents a roughly eighteen-fold increase from the neonatal mass. The interplay between delayed first breeding, markedly low annual reproductive output, and exceptional longevity reflects energetic constraints typical of large psittacines inhabiting the resource-poor Caatinga, where the probability of adult survival must be maximized at the expense of annual fecundity. Historical field data from the last known wild individual, observed in the 1980s and 1990s, generally support these projections, though captive records suggest that some individuals may persist for up to 7 years beyond this figure, a difference that some authors attribute to inbreeding depression in the wild lineage rather than intrinsic physiological limits.
